video_title: Should You Pick Stocks or Buy Index Funds? | ATC
gist: A live listener-mailbag episode taped at the Future Proof conference, with Alex Morris of FM Investments arguing that 5%+ high-quality bond yields are a genuine math-driven opportunity on the day the Fed hiked 25bp and signaled another, Barry pushing back on the 'boomers will crash the market' thesis and capping speculative 'cowboy accounts' at 5%, and Bill Sweet covering asset location inside IRAs. Despite the title, the stock-picking-vs-indexing debate is only one segment among bonds, inflation, generational wealth transfer, luxury watches as an asset class, and whether to hire an adviser.

themes.theme: 5% bond yields and how they actually pay out

insights.claim: High-quality bond index funds are yielding over 5% average yield to maturity, a level not seen in more than a decade, which the hosts frame as an attractive absolute entry point versus the 2010s and early 2020s.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson (host)
insights.so_what: Investors who dismissed fixed income during the ZIRP era now have a math-based alternative to equities without taking equity risk.
insights.quote: if you just look at the A, any sort of bond index fund, any sort of high quality something, it's yielding over 5% average yield of maturity. We haven't had that in a very long time.

insights.claim: A quoted 5.2% bond yield is only realized if the bond does not default and is held to maturity, and it arrives as semiannual coupons plus principal at the end, not as a smooth 5.2% return each year.
insights.speaker: Alex Morris (FM Investments)
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations: individual bond buyers should not expect annual mark-to-market returns matching the headline yield.
insights.quote: if you're an individual investor and you see 5.2% 2% yield and you buy that bond, you will get that number assuming it a doesn't default and b you hold it to maturity

insights.claim: Bond ETFs never mature: they rebalance weekly, monthly or quarterly to maintain constant duration against a benchmark and reinvest maturing proceeds at whatever rate prevails, so an ETF holder does not lock in today's yield the way a single bond holder does.
insights.speaker: Alex Morris (FM Investments)
insights.so_what: Investors wanting a guaranteed 5% should use individual bonds or defined-maturity products rather than assuming an ETF locks the rate in.

insights.claim: Bonds do not trade on a lit market the way equities do, so retail buyers get different prices from different dealers depending on inventory constraints and pay platform fees, with very little free bond trading at Schwab or Fidelity compared with stocks.
insights.speaker: Alex Morris (FM Investments)
insights.so_what: Execution costs are a hidden drag on individual bond buying and a practical argument for using funds or ETFs instead.
insights.quote: Bonds don't trade on a lighted market in the same way that stocks do where you can say this is the exact price of Apple at the MBBO today.

themes.theme: Fed hikes, inflation and the TIPS answer

insights.claim: The Fed raised rates 25 basis points on the day of taping and, per the dot plot, signaled another 25 basis point move by the end of the year, with Chair Kevin Warsh closing the statement with the words 'the committee will deliver price stability.'
insights.speaker: Alex Morris (FM Investments)
insights.so_what: A hiking, inflation-fighting Fed means short-duration and inflation-linked instruments carry the near-term advantage over long duration.
insights.quote: the last six words of the statement that Kevin Worsh gave today and gave last time, the committee will deliver price stability

insights.claim: If you genuinely believe inflation will stay near 3.5% permanently, equities rather than nominal bonds are the right vehicle because inflation stokes equity values over the long run, but that bet is directly opposed by a Fed with a massive balance sheet committed to a 2% target.
insights.speaker: Alex Morris (FM Investments)
insights.so_what: Frames the inflation view as the single fork in the road determining stocks-versus-bonds allocation, and warns against fighting the Fed's stated reaction function.
insights.quote: The Fed, given its massive balance sheet, is actually now betting against you if that's the bet you're going to do.

insights.claim: The current high-rate environment is self-terminating by design: the Fed is raising rates specifically to slow growth and inflation, and if it succeeds rates fall, which mechanically reverses the price losses bond funds took on the way up.
insights.speaker: Alex Morris (FM Investments)
insights.so_what: Argues that the mark-to-market pain in bond funds is the setup for the total-return payoff, favoring adding duration rather than abandoning it.
insights.quote: It it not just could. The goal is it will. If it doesn't, the Fed will have failed miserably in its job.

insights.claim: TIPS are the government's direct answer for investors who want bond-like return without inflation risk, and FM Investments' RBIL is pitched as the only ultra-short-duration TIPS product on the market, currently paying closer to 4% because it tracks the cash rate.
insights.speaker: Alex Morris (FM Investments)
insights.so_what: A specific, named instrument for expressing an inflation-hedged cash allocation, though it is the guest's own product.
insights.quote: You got to take a look at our bill RBIL. It's the only ultra short duration tips product on the market.

themes.theme: Boomer wealth and the market-crash myth

insights.claim: Baby boomers hold roughly $90 trillion of the $174 trillion of US household wealth per Fed data, with another $20 trillion in the silent generation that will largely flow to boomers, meaning about two-thirds of national wealth sits with older Americans.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson (host)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the demographic concentration underlying both the 'boomers will crash the market' fear and the coming wealth-transfer opportunity.
insights.quote: according to the Fed, $90 trillion out of 174 trillion in USA is owned by the baby boomers

insights.claim: The claim that boomer retirement accounts are propping up the market is the same error as the 'cash on the sidelines' story, because every stock sale simply swaps who holds the cash and who holds the shares, leaving the aggregate unchanged.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson (host)
insights.so_what: Kills a recurring bullish and bearish talking point; flows narratives based on aggregate cash or demographics should be discounted.
insights.quote: So, there's still the same million dollars on the sideline. So, that doesn't work.

insights.claim: Stepped-up cost basis at death removes the tax-forced-selling channel entirely: heirs receive appreciated portfolios at a new high basis with no tax hit until they sell, so there is no reason for them to hit the bid.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: The mechanical case against a demographic sell-off; policy change to stepped-up basis would be the actual risk trigger to watch.
insights.quote: there's no reason to hit the bid because they can let that appreciate and they're starting at a very high level

insights.claim: Boomers have been retiring at roughly 10,000 people a day for years without producing the predicted market crash, and the cohort spans an 18-year birth range starting in 1946, so any selling is spread across nearly two decades rather than concentrated.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: Demographic doom theses are already years into their supposed trigger window and have repeatedly failed to play out.
insights.quote: Boomers were retiring 10,000 people a day. This has been going on for years.

insights.claim: US housing remains supply-constrained because 3 to 5 million single-family homes were underbuilt after the financial crisis, and boomers are de-risking portfolios but not yet downsizing their houses, so that backlog stays a problem until they move.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: Structural housing shortage supports home prices; the release valve is boomer downsizing in the 2030s, when Gen Z is expected to be the buyer.
insights.quote: following the financial crisis, we underbuilt single family homes, depending on which study you want to believe, 3, four, 5 million houses

insights.claim: A speculative 'cowboy account' should be capped at about 5% of a portfolio or less, so a win is still meaningful while a total loss does not affect standard of living, making a 15-20% speculative sleeve too large.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: A concrete sizing rule for the behavioral-hack sleeve that lets investors satisfy the stock-picking itch without endangering the core.
insights.quote: So I like the idea of 5% or less. So if it does well it's meaningful and if it crashes and burns it doesn't affect your standard of living.

insights.claim: A speculative sleeve consumes mental bandwidth wildly out of proportion to its size: the guest reports his own cowboy account is under 2% of his portfolio yet absorbs roughly half his personal investing attention, which is precisely its function as a decoy from the real money.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: Reframes the speculative sleeve as a deliberate attention sink rather than a return generator, and warns that the time cost is real.
insights.quote: I looked at it and I'm like, "Oh my god, this is like less than 2% of my portfolio." And when I think about my personal account, this is probably half of my mental bandwidth.

insights.claim: Active manager persistence collapses with horizon: fewer than half beat their benchmark in any given year, about 20% over five years, under 10% over ten years, and only a handful over twenty years, naming Buffett, Lynch and Danoff as the exceptions.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: The base rates argue for sizing any stock-picking sleeve as entertainment, not as an expected-alpha allocation.

insights.claim: Citing Ken French, you cannot distinguish luck from skill in an investment record until it spans 20 years, so even a decade of outperformance from something like an overweight in semiconductors proves nothing.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: A discipline for evaluating both your own track record and hot managers: demand two decades and risk-adjusted numbers before attributing skill.
insights.quote: We don't know if someone is lucky or skillful until they have a 20-year track record.

insights.claim: Survivorship distortion runs through anecdotal stock-picking evidence: the guest says investors who approach him proudly show 40-year portfolios built by buying in 1987, 2000 and 2008-09, while the thousand others show bankrupt tickers with a five-letter Q symbol they refuse to sell.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: Explains why visible stock-picking success stories systematically overstate the odds, and flags the buy-the-crash behavior that actually drove the winners.
insights.quote: No, no one brags about the losses.

themes.theme: Collectibles as a pseudo asset class

insights.claim: Watches, collectible cars, art and wine effectively became an asset class after 2020 when bored consumers with cash and no sports to watch bid prices up, a dynamic the hosts label a bull market phenomenon rather than a durable one.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: Treat collectible price appreciation as a liquidity-and-boredom artifact that can reverse, not a structural return stream.
insights.quote: Cuz people had cash. They didn't know what to do. They were bored. There was no sports on TV. Let's buy a Rolley.

insights.claim: Within watches, value retention is bifurcated: less-desired references like the Milgauss trade 20-30% below list on secondary platforms such as Chrono24 and Hodinkee, while precious-metal models hold value largely because gold at $4,000-$5,000 an ounce accounts for about half the piece's worth.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: The only reliable floor under a luxury watch is its metal content, which ties collectible pricing to the gold trade.
insights.quote: half the value of the watch is $4,000 $5,000 an ounce gold

insights.claim: A high-income professional with $200,000 of student debt at 7-9% and negative net worth should pay down debt and build the practice and portfolio first, buying meaningful sub-$3,000 watches now and reserving a $20,000-25,000 purchase for a professional milestone rather than a flex.
insights.speaker: Barry (guest adviser)
insights.so_what: A spending permission rule: discretionary luxury is fine once the plan is funded and the high-rate debt is handled.
insights.quote: rather than have him go out and spend 20 $25,000 on a watch. I would much rather see someone like this doctor pay down that debt, especially if it's 7 8 9%

insights.claim: Tax-loss harvesting and holding-period discipline are meaningless inside rollover IRAs because all distributions come out as ordinary income regardless, which is also what gives IRAs complete freedom to trade without tax friction.
insights.speaker: Bill Sweet
insights.so_what: Redirects effort from pointless in-IRA tax gymnastics toward a distribution plan and asset placement.
insights.quote: Ain't no Ain't no such thing. That dog will not hunt.

insights.claim: Asset location argues for holding bonds and high-turnover trend-following strategies inside tax-qualified accounts, since bond income is taxed as ordinary income anyway and trend strategies trade in and out without triggering gains in an IRA.
insights.speaker: Bill Sweet
insights.so_what: A concrete placement rule that raises after-tax return without changing the underlying allocation.
insights.quote: Bonds, you're paying ordinary income anyway. That's a great place to hold bonds.

insights.claim: Citing a possibly apocryphal Fidelity study, the two groups that outperformed everyone else were investors who had moved and stopped receiving account statements and investors who had died, evidence that trading activity is a detriment rather than a proxy for returns.
insights.speaker: Bill Sweet
insights.so_what: The strongest behavioral argument for automating and ignoring a portfolio, and for treating engagement as a cost.
insights.quote: So, paradoxically, activity is not a proxy for better returns. In fact, usually it's a detriment.

insights.claim: Hiring an adviser is not a binary choice against staying educated: good advisers should teach clients, and an investor can outsource tax, estate and downside-risk expertise while keeping engagement with markets, so an adviser who does not educate should be replaced.
insights.speaker: Ben Carlson (host)
insights.so_what: Gives self-directed investors a screening criterion for advisers and removes the perceived cost of giving up hands-on learning.
insights.quote: If you have an adviser who's not educating you, you have to find someone else.
